metadata.description:
Mexico City, one of the largest cities in the world, is sinking, in some areas by tens of centimeters every year. How can a whole city sink?

In this video: the Aztec capital built on an island in a lake, how the Spanish and later governments drained that lake, the soft clay left behind, the groundwater pumped from beneath the city, why a city built on a lake now struggles both with floods and with water shortages, and what can be done.
metadata.pinned_comment: Have you ever noticed the tilting buildings in Mexico City's historic center? 👇

scenes.narration: This is Mexico City. With more than twenty million people in its metropolitan area, it's one of the biggest cities on Earth.
And it's sinking. Not by a little. In some neighborhoods, the ground drops by tens of centimeters every single year.

data.text: Sinking by tens of centimeters a year

scenes.narration: Churches lean. Streets crack. Old buildings that once stood at street level now sit below it, or rise above it.

data.text: Churches lean. Streets crack.

scenes.narration: The strangest part? Five hundred years ago, most of this ground was underwater.
So why is Mexico City sinking?

data.text: Why is Mexico City sinking?

chapters.title: A city in a bowl
chapters.title_youtube: A city in a mountain bowl

scenes.narration: By the end of this video, you'll see how an island city, a drained lake, a layer of soft clay and millions of thirsty people are pulling the ground down.

data.text: An island, a lost lake, soft clay and a thirsty city

scenes.narration: Around twenty-two million people live in the Mexico City metropolitan area. That's more than the whole population of countries like Chile or the Netherlands.
And it sits high up. The city center is about two thousand two hundred and forty meters above sea level, higher than many ski resorts in the Alps.
At that altitude, the air is thinner. Each breath holds roughly a quarter less oxygen than at sea level, something visiting athletes notice immediately.

data.text: A quarter less oxygen in every breath

scenes.narration: It lies in a high valley, the Valley of Mexico, surrounded on all sides by mountains and volcanoes.
To the south-east rises Popocatépetl, an active volcano more than five thousand four hundred meters high. On clear days, you can see it from the city.

data.caption: an active volcano next to the city

scenes.narration: Here's the key fact. This valley is a closed basin. No river naturally drains it to the sea. Rain that falls here has nowhere to go.

data.text: A valley with no natural exit

scenes.narration: So for thousands of years, water collected at the bottom of the valley, forming a chain of shallow lakes. And as rivers washed in fine mud, it settled on the lake floor.

data.title: How the valley filled with lakes

scenes.narration: Over thousands of years, that mud built up into a thick layer of very soft clay. Remember that clay. It's the hidden villain of this story.

data.text: A thick layer of very soft clay

scenes.narration: Long before the Aztecs, this valley was already home to great cities. Teotihuacan, north-east of the lakes, was one of the largest cities in the Americas around the year 500.

data.text: An ancient valley of great cities

scenes.narration: There wasn't just one lake. A chain of connected lakes ran across the valley floor. The northern lakes were salty, while the southern ones, like Xochimilco and Chalco, were fed by springs and had fresher water.

data.text: A chain of lakes, salty and fresh

scenes.narration: When the Spanish arrived in 1519, the largest of these lakes, Lake Texcoco, covered much of the valley floor. And in the middle of it was a city.
According to tradition, the Mexica, the people we often call the Aztecs, founded their city on a small island in the lake around 1325.
Their legend says the gods told them to settle where they saw an eagle on a cactus, eating a snake. That image is still in the center of Mexico's flag today.

data.text: An eagle on a cactus

scenes.narration: The island was a smart choice. It was easy to defend, and canoes could carry goods across the lake from every town on its shores.

data.text: Easy to defend, easy to supply by canoe

scenes.narration: Its great market, at Tlatelolco, amazed the Spanish. Their chroniclers described tens of thousands of people buying and selling there on a single day.

data.text: A market for tens of thousands

scenes.narration: One Spanish soldier, Bernal Díaz del Castillo, later wrote that when they first saw the city rising from the water, some of them wondered if they were dreaming.

data.text: Some wondered if they were dreaming

scenes.narration: To grow food, they built chinampas: narrow artificial islands made of mud and plants, piled up in the shallow water and anchored by trees.

data.text: Farms built on the lake itself

scenes.narration: Chinampas were incredibly productive, with water always at hand. Some still exist today in Xochimilco, in the south of the city, and they are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

data.text: The last of the floating gardens

scenes.narration: The city was connected to the shore by long causeways built across the water, with bridges that could be removed in case of attack.
Part of the lake was salty. So the Aztecs built a long dike, more than ten kilometers long, to separate fresher water around the city from the salty water to the east.

data.text: A wall to keep the salty water out

scenes.narration: The dike was built in the mid fourteen hundreds, after a disastrous flood, and its design is traditionally credited to Nezahualcoyotl, the poet-king of the nearby city of Texcoco.

data.text: A poet-king who engineered a lake

scenes.narration: Fresh drinking water came by aqueduct from the springs of Chapultepec, on the western shore.

data.text: Drinking water by aqueduct

scenes.narration: By 1519, Tenochtitlan may have had around two hundred thousand people, making it one of the largest cities in the world at the time.

data.caption: one of the largest cities on Earth

scenes.narration: The Aztecs lived with the lake. They built on it, farmed on it, and traveled across it. What came next would do the opposite.

data.text: They lived with the lake

scenes.narration: In 1521, after a long siege, Spanish forces led by Hernán Cortés and their Indigenous allies conquered Tenochtitlan. The city was largely destroyed.
The Spanish built their new capital right on top of the ruins. But they built it like a European city: streets instead of canals, carts instead of canoes.

data.text: A European city on top of a lake

scenes.narration: The dikes and canals that controlled the water fell apart. And during heavy rainy seasons, the lake rose and flooded the city.

data.text: The lake kept coming back

scenes.narration: The worst flood began in 1629. Parts of the city stayed underwater for about five years.
So the colonial government decided the lake was the enemy. If the valley had no exit, they would make one.

data.text: If the valley had no exit, make one

scenes.narration: After the great flood, there were even serious discussions about moving the capital to higher ground. In the end, the city stayed, and chose to fight the water instead.

data.text: Move the capital, or fight the water?

scenes.narration: Starting in 1607, workers dug a tunnel, and later a huge open cut, through the hills in the north of the valley, to let water flow out toward the Gulf of Mexico.
Drainage went on for centuries. In 1900, the Gran Canal was completed. Then, from 1975, deep drainage tunnels were dug far beneath the city.
The first tunnel was designed by an engineer called Enrico Martínez. It often collapsed and clogged, and it took generations of work to turn it into a working drain.

data.text: Generations of work to drain one valley

scenes.narration: The Gran Canal, finished under President Porfirio Díaz, ran for about forty-seven kilometers to carry the valley's water and sewage north.

data.text: A 47-kilometer canal

scenes.narration: Little by little, Lake Texcoco disappeared. Today, only small remnants of the old lake system are left.
On the dry lakebed, the city grew and grew, especially in the twentieth century, when millions of people moved here from the countryside.

data.text: A city spreading across the old lakebed

scenes.narration: In 1900, the city had around half a million people. By 2020, the metropolitan area had more than twenty-one million.
And all those people needed water. The lake was gone. So the city looked down, under its own feet.

data.text: The city looked under its own feet

scenes.narration: If you're enjoying this, subscribe. Every week we find the story hidden in another map.

data.text: Subscribe for a new map story every week

scenes.narration: Under the valley lies an aquifer: layers of sand and gravel soaked with water, like a giant underground sponge.

data.text: A giant sponge under the city

scenes.narration: From the late eighteen hundreds, and especially in the twentieth century, the city drilled thousands of wells into it.

data.text: Thousands of wells

scenes.narration: As the water table dropped, wells had to be drilled deeper and deeper, often hundreds of meters down, to keep reaching the water.

data.text: Wells drilled deeper and deeper

scenes.narration: Today, most of the city's water still comes from wells, pumped from the aquifer beneath it. Estimates usually put it at around six out of every ten liters.
The problem is balance. Every year, much more water is pumped out than rain can put back in.
And the city makes refilling harder. Concrete and asphalt cover the old lakebed, so rain that once soaked into the ground now runs into the drains.

data.text: Concrete stops the rain soaking in

scenes.narration: Now remember that clay. The old lakebed clay is incredibly soft, and it's full of water. In places, it's more water than solid.

data.text: Clay that is mostly water

scenes.narration: When water is pumped from the layers below, water drains out of the clay too. And when the clay loses its water, it shrinks and compacts. The ground on top sinks.

data.title: Why pumping makes the city sink

scenes.narration: Think of a wet sponge under a heavy book. Squeeze the water out, and the sponge gets thinner. Except this sponge is the ground beneath twenty million people.

data.text: A squeezed sponge under a city

scenes.narration: And here's the worst part. Once the clay is compacted, it doesn't spring back. Even if the aquifer refilled, most of the lost height would never return.

data.text: The lost height never comes back

scenes.narration: Scientists noticed the sinking more than a century ago. By the 1950s, engineers had clearly linked it to the pumping of groundwater.

data.text: Linked to pumping since the 1950s

scenes.narration: So how much has it sunk? Since the early twentieth century, some parts of the city have dropped by around ten meters. That's the height of a three-story building.
Satellites now measure it with great precision. In the fastest-sinking areas, the ground is dropping by up to around thirty to forty centimeters a year.

data.caption: per year, in the worst areas

scenes.narration: The measurements come from satellite radar, which can detect changes in the height of the ground of just millimeters, from hundreds of kilometers up in space.

data.text: Measuring millimeters from space

scenes.narration: For comparison, global sea level is rising by a few millimeters a year. Parts of Mexico City are sinking roughly a hundred times faster.

data.text: About a hundred times faster than sea level rise

scenes.narration: You can see it in the city's most famous monument. The Angel of Independence, built in 1910, stands on deep foundations. So as the street around it sank, the column seemed to rise.

data.text: A monument that seemed to rise

scenes.narration: To reach its base, fourteen extra steps have had to be added over the years.

data.caption: as the ground sank around it

scenes.narration: In some places, metal well casings anchored deep in firm ground now stick out of the pavement, because the ground around them has dropped away.

data.text: Wells sticking out of the pavement

scenes.narration: The Palace of Fine Arts, a huge building clad in heavy marble, has sunk noticeably since it was built. You can see that its entrance sits lower than the streets around it.

data.text: A marble palace sinking under its own weight

scenes.narration: The Metropolitan Cathedral, on the main square, began leaning as different parts of its foundation sank at different speeds. In the 1990s, engineers carefully removed soil from under the higher parts to straighten it.

data.text: A cathedral that had to be straightened

scenes.narration: That's the real danger: uneven sinking. When one side of a building drops faster than the other, walls crack and floors tilt.

data.text: Uneven sinking cracks buildings

scenes.narration: Water pipes break as the ground shifts under them. Roads crack. And the metro and drainage tunnels must constantly be repaired.

data.text: Pipes break, roads crack, tunnels shift

scenes.narration: The soft clay also amplifies earthquakes. Seismic waves can shake much harder on the old lakebed than on solid rock just a few kilometers away.

data.text: Soft clay makes earthquakes stronger

scenes.narration: And the sinking isn't the same everywhere. It's fastest where the clay is thickest, on the old lakebed in the east. On the rocky hills around the edges, it's much slower.

chapters.title: Floods and thirst
chapters.title_youtube: Too much water, and not enough

scenes.narration: Here's the paradox. A city that was once a lake now suffers from two problems at once: floods, and not enough water.

data.text: Floods and thirst at the same time

scenes.narration: As the city sinks, its drains lose their slope. Water that once flowed downhill out of the valley now has to be pumped uphill, out of a growing bowl.

data.text: Drains that now run uphill

scenes.narration: So the city keeps building bigger tunnels. The Emisor Oriente, opened in 2019, is a drainage tunnel about sixty-two kilometers long.

data.text: A 62-kilometer drainage tunnel

scenes.narration: Much of the city's wastewater flows north, out of the valley, into the state of Hidalgo, where it has long been used to irrigate farmland. A huge treatment plant at Atotonilco now cleans part of it.

data.text: Wastewater that waters distant farms

scenes.narration: Meanwhile, the wells can't supply everyone. So the city also brings water from outside the valley, through the Cutzamala System.

data.text: Water from outside the valley

scenes.narration: Its reservoirs lie more than a hundred kilometers to the west. The water has to be pumped uphill by more than a thousand meters to reach the city. That takes enormous amounts of electricity.
In 2024, after years of drought, the Cutzamala reservoirs fell to record lows, and many neighborhoods were left depending on water trucks.

data.text: Reservoirs at record lows

scenes.narration: And a large share of the water is lost before it arrives. Old pipes, many cracked by the sinking ground, leak an estimated forty percent of it.
That creates a vicious circle. Leaks mean more pumping. More pumping means more sinking. More sinking means more broken pipes, and more leaks.
Every rainy season, huge amounts of rain still fall on the city. But most of it is sent away through the drains, while wells pump water up from below.

data.text: Rain sent away, water pumped up

scenes.narration: During summer storms, heavy rain can fall in a short time, and streets on the lowest parts of the old lakebed still flood regularly.

data.text: Summer storms still flood the lowest streets

scenes.narration: So can Mexico City stop sinking? Not completely, at least not soon. But it can slow down.

data.text: It can't stop, but it can slow down

scenes.narration: The solutions are simple to describe and hard to do: fix the leaking pipes, pump less from the aquifer, and help more rain soak back into the ground.
Some projects already collect rainwater from rooftops, especially in poorer neighborhoods that get little water from the network.

data.text: Catching the rain on rooftops

scenes.narration: Engineers are also studying ways to inject treated water back into the aquifer, to refill the giant sponge instead of only emptying it.

data.text: Refilling the sponge

scenes.narration: And in Xochimilco, farmers still grow vegetables and flowers on chinampas, using the same technique the Aztecs used centuries ago. Living with the water, not against it.

data.text: Living with the water, not against it

scenes.narration: On part of the dry bed of Lake Texcoco, where a huge new airport was once planned, a large ecological park and wetlands are being restored.

data.text: Bringing some water back to the lakebed

scenes.narration: Mexico City isn't alone. Other cities on soft ground that pump too much groundwater, like Jakarta in Indonesia, are sinking for the same reason.

data.text: A problem shared by other cities

scenes.narration: That's why engineers around the world study Mexico City as a warning: this is what happens when a city takes much more water from the ground than nature can give back.

data.text: A warning for cities everywhere

scenes.narration: But nowhere is the story clearer than here, in a city that turned a lake into land, and is now paying the price, centimeter by centimeter.

data.text: Centimeter by centimeter

scenes.narration: So let's put the whole story together.

data.text: Putting the whole story together

scenes.narration: Mexico City sits in a closed valley that was once filled with lakes. Over thousands of years, those lakes left behind a thick layer of soft, water-filled clay.

data.title: Why Mexico City is sinking
items: A closed valley full of lakes

scenes.narration: Then the lake was drained, a giant city grew on top, and millions of people began pumping water from below. As the clay dries out, it compacts, and the city sinks.
The Aztecs built a city that lived with the lake. Five hundred years later, the lake is gone. But the ground still remembers it.
